analysis.one_liner: Bans interstate and foreign commerce in steel jaw leghold traps and fur from animals caught in them.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in April 1996 and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which took no further action before the 104th Congress ended, so it never received a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it a federal crime to ship steel jaw leghold traps across state lines or national borders, or to trade any fur taken from an animal caught in one. Violators would face fines, and repeat violators up to two years in prison; the Interior Department could seize illegal traps and furs, pay informers half of any fine collected, and seek court orders to stop violators. The ban would take effect one year after enactment. It never left committee, so nothing in it became law.
analysis.who_benefits: Wild animals caught in leghold traps, pets and other non-target animals that get snapped by traps set for fur-bearing species, and people who want cruel trapping methods restricted. The bill does not ban trapping outright or possession of traps; it cuts off the commerce that moves traps and leghold-trapped fur across state and national lines [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Animals and people opposed to leghold traps

how_it_helps.text: The bill declares US policy to be ending the 'needless maiming and suffering' inflicted on animals by steel jaw leghold traps, and implements that by prohibiting shipment of the traps and of fur from animals caught in them in interstate or foreign commerce [S2][S3].

It backs the ban with criminal fines of up to $1,000 for a first violation and up to $5,000, two years in prison, or both for repeat violations, and subjects illegal traps and fur to government forfeiture [S2][S3].
It directs the Secretary of the Interior to reward informers 50 percent of any fine collected from a conviction, giving the public a direct financial stake in enforcement [S2][S3].
Enforcement officials could detain, search, and seize suspected traps or furs, make arrests with or without warrants, and the Attorney General could seek injunctions against violators [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Trappers who sell leghold-trapped fur, fur buyers and dealers, and manufacturers and sellers of steel jaw leghold traps, who would lose a legal market for their products. Consumers of fur products could face higher prices or reduced supply of domestically leghold-trapped fur. The bill gives a one-year lead time before the ban takes effect [S3].

drawbacks.text: The ban reaches commerce but not possession or use within a state, so animals could still be caught in leghold traps within a single state, and the bill's practical effect depends entirely on how aggressively the Interior Department and federal prosecutors enforce it [S3].

The penalties are modest — a $1,000 maximum fine for a first offense — which critics of animal welfare laws have argued is too small to deter an industry; meanwhile the enforcement powers, including warrantless arrests and informant rewards, expand government search and seizure authority [S3].

Fur trappers and rural communities where trapping is a livelihood would bear the cost, and the ban on imported leghold-trapped fur could raise prices for fur buyers without stopping trapping in countries that export to the US unless enforcement deters imports.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would impose a real cost on a small, specific industry — trappers and fur dealers who rely on steel jaw leghold traps — in exchange for ending a practice widely viewed as inflicting prolonged suffering on trapped animals, including pets caught unintentionally. The tradeoff is narrow and deliberate: it targets one trap type and one commerce channel rather than all trapping. The main weakness is enforcement, since modest fines and a commerce-only reach may leave gaps.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee in April 1996, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended, so it died without any vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Claiborne Pell of Rhode Island introduced S. 1701 on April 24, 1996, and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor [S1][S5].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works [S5].
Three Democratic senators cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did [S4].
No further action appears in the bill's history: the committee never held a markup or reported the bill, and the full Senate never voted on it before the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Trappers, fur dealers, and trap manufacturers are better off, since the commerce ban they would have faced never advanced; no one else gains materially from the bill's failure.

industries.industry: Fur trappers and the fur trade
industries.note: The bill would bar any fur taken with a steel jaw leghold trap from interstate or foreign commerce, cutting off the market for leghold-trapped pelts. Trappers would have to switch methods or lose access to buyers outside their state.
Shipping, selling, or even receiving a steel jaw leghold trap that crossed state lines would become a federal crime, effectively ending the national market for the product.

industries.industry: Importers and exporters of fur garments
industries.note: Import and export of fur articles derived from leghold-trapped animals would be prohibited, forcing foreign supply chains to certify trap methods or lose the US market.
